newsitem.title: JAPAN: Fire caused explosion at Japan nuclear plant.
newsitem.headline: Fire caused explosion at Japan nuclear plant.

text.p: A fire which caused radiation to escape from Japan's only nuclear reprocessing plant was not extinguished properly and caused an explosion at the facility 10 hours later, the operators said on Wednesday.
The accident on Tuesday, which contaminated 21 workers with low-level radiation, cast a cloud over Japan's nuclear power industry, which provides one-third of the country's electricity.
Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto formally apologised to the nation over the accident and environmental groups seized on it as a reason why the nuclear industry could not be trusted.
The accident forced the state-run Power Reactor and Nuclear Fuel Development Corporation (PNC) to shut down the complex at Tokaimura, 160 km (100 miles) northeast of Tokyo.
Some radiation leaked from the plant but at levels far below those that would pose health risks to the public, a PNC spokesman said.
There were no evacuations and contaminated workers were allowed to go home with a clean bill of health, he added.
Tokaimura residents, who are heavily dependant on the plant for work, said they were not angered by the accident and pointed out that life was back to normal with schools and shops all open.

A senior PNC official told reporters on Wednesday that the fire at the bituminisation facility for low-level nuclear waste, a building near the main reprocessing plant, was not extinguished properly and this caused the later explosion.
Investigators in protective clothing and carrying geiger counters had not so far determined the reason for the fire.
The explosion 10 hours later at about 8 p.m. blew out a steel door sealing the main room and severely damaged other parts of the building, the PNC official said.
The facility is used to mix irradiated low-level liquid waste, a by-product of the main spent nuclear fuel reprocessing plant, with asphalt, for storage in drums.
The Tokaimura plant is Japan's only nuclear reprocessing facility, extracting plutonium from spent nuclear fuel.
The plant reprocesses about 12 percent of spent nuclear fuel from Japan's 50 running commercial nuclear power plants, with the rest reprocessed at French plants.
Prime Minister Hashimoto criticised the PNC's slow and "inadequate" first reports of the accident.

"What I regret most is the fact that the PNC did not provide an adequate and speedy report on the fire and radiation leak after having been exposed to severe public criticism of its conduct over the Monju affair," Hashimoto told parliament.

In December 1995, the PNC came under criticism over the cover-up of a massive coolant leak at Monju, Japan's only fast-breeder reactor. Although the accident at Monju did not leak radiation, the reactor remains closed.
A PNC official at Monju committed suicide after the media revealed he tried to keep video tapes of the accident secret.

"We deeply regret that Tuesday's accident caused concern among residents," PNC chairman Toshiyuki Kondo told a news conference. "I do not think there was a cover-up but I admit there was a delay in our report to the government."
Anti-nuclear groups said the PNC was not to be trusted.
"I have grave doubts about the announced levels of radiation," said Jinzaburo Takagi, a physicist and leader of the anti-nuclear group Citizen's Nuclear Information Centre.
The environmental group Greenpeace criticised the PNC for not immediately reporting the seriousness of the fire.
"The health impact on local residents could be very serious," Greenpeace said in a statement. "The PNC should have let residents evacuate as soon as possible."
